questions.prompt: The Hessian of a scalar function is
questions.explanation: Each entry is one second partial derivative: row i and column j holds the derivative of the i-th partial with respect to the j-th coordinate. The column of first partials is the gradient. A Jacobian belongs to a vector-valued map; the Hessian is the Jacobian of the gradient. The sum of the diagonal entries is the trace, one number, not the matrix.

the column of first partial derivatives
the Jacobian of an arbitrary vector-valued map

questions.prompt: Let \(f(x, y) = x^3 y + 2 y^2 + 5 x y\). At \((1, 2)\), what is \(\partial^2 f / \partial x^2\)?
questions.explanation: The first partial in \(x\) is \(3 x^2 y + 5 y\). Differentiating again in \(x\) gives \(6 x y\), which equals \(6 \cdot 1 \cdot 2 = 12\). The mixed partial \(3 x^2 + 5\) equals 8 at this point. The pure second partial in \(y\) is 4. The first partial in \(x\), evaluated here, is \(6 + 10 = 16\), and that is a first derivative.

questions.prompt: For a function with continuous second partials, the mixed entries satisfy
questions.explanation: Continuous second partials may be taken in either order, so the Hessian is symmetric. The mixed entry is not forced to vanish, and it is not equal to a first partial. Symmetry does not force the off-diagonal entries to be zero, so the matrix need not be diagonal.

\(\partial^2 f / \partial x \partial y = \partial^2 f / \partial y \partial x\)
\(\partial^2 f / \partial x \partial y = \partial f / \partial x\)
the Hessian is diagonal

questions.prompt: For \(f = a x^2 y + b x y^2\), the mixed partial \(\partial^2 f / \partial y \partial x\) is an expression in the names a, b, x, and y. Write that expression.
questions.explanation:
The partial derivative in \(x\) is \(2 a x y + b y^2\). Differentiating that in \(y\) gives \(2 a x + 2 b y\). Differentiating first in \(y\) and then in \(x\) produces the same expression.
• \(2 a x\) drops the second summand.
• \(a x^2 + 2 b x y\) is a first partial, not the mixed second partial.
• \(2 a + 2 b\) differentiates the remaining variables away.

questions.prompt: Let \(f(x, y) = x^3 y + 2 y^2 + 5 x y\). At \((1, 2)\), what is the mixed partial \(\partial^2 f / \partial y \partial x\)?
questions.explanation: From \(3 x^2 y + 5 y\), differentiating in \(y\) gives \(3 x^2 + 5\), which equals 8 at \(x = 1\). The pure second partial in \(x\) is 12, and the pure second partial in \(y\) is 4. The product \(3 \cdot 1 + 5 \cdot 2 = 13\) treats the expression as if both factors were still present after differentiation.

questions.prompt: At \((1, 2)\) the Hessian of \(f(x, y) = x^3 y + 2 y^2 + 5 x y\) is \(\begin{bmatrix} 12 & 8 \\ 8 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\). What is \(v^{T} H v\) for \(v = (1, 0)\)?
questions.explanation: The quadratic form on the first basis vector is the \((1, 1)\) entry, 12. The other diagonal entry is 4, which is the quadratic form on \((0, 1)\). The sum of all four entries is 32, which is the quadratic form on \((1, 1)\). The off-diagonal entry 8 does not appear in \(v^{T} H v\) when the second coordinate of \(v\) is 0.

questions.prompt: One step below is false. Select that step, and the reason it fails. The function is \(f(x, y) = x^2 y\).
questions.explanation: The first three steps are the right partial derivatives: \(f_x = 2 x y\), \(f_{xy} = 2 x\), and \(f_y = x^2\). The derivative of \(x^2\) with respect to \(x\) is \(2x\), not \(x\). Both mixed partials equal \(2x\), so they agree. The false step is the differentiation, not a failure of symmetry.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>second-derivative positions</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">xx   xy</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">yx   yy</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 array labeled by second-derivative positions.
steps: The first partial derivative with respect to x is 2 x y.
Differentiating that partial derivative with respect to y gives 2 x.
The first partial derivative with respect to y is x squared.
Differentiating x squared with respect to x gives x, so the mixed partials disagree.
reasons: The derivative of x squared is 2x, so both mixed partials equal 2x.
A polynomial is allowed to have mixed partials that disagree.
The first partial derivative with respect to x should have been x squared.

questions.prompt: Using the Hessian \(\begin{bmatrix} 12 & 8 \\ 8 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\) at \((1, 2)\), what is \(v^{T} H v\) for \(v = (1, 1)\)?
questions.explanation: \(H v = (20, 12)\), and the inner product with \((1, 1)\) is \(20 + 12 = 32\). The same total is \(12 + 8 + 8 + 4\). The trace is \(12 + 4 = 16\), which drops the off-diagonal contributions. The determinant is \(48 - 64 = -16\), a different summary of the matrix.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>second-derivative positions</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">xx   xy</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">yx   yy</text></svg>

questions.prompt: The second derivative of \(t \mapsto f(x + t d)\), at \(t = 0\), equals
questions.explanation: The first derivative of the slice is the gradient dotted with \(d\). Differentiating again brings down the Hessian and leaves the quadratic form \(d^{T} H d\). The trace sums curvatures in the coordinate directions, not in the direction \(d\). The length of \(H d\) is not the second derivative of the slice.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.
options: \(\nabla f(x)^{T} d\)
the trace of the Hessian
\(\lVert H_f(x)\, d \rVert\)

questions.prompt: Which statements hold for the Hessian?
questions.explanation: Continuous second partials commute, so the matrix is symmetric, and the slice's second derivative is the quadratic form of that matrix. A linear function has second partials equal to 0, so its Hessian is the zero matrix, not the identity. Equality of mixed partials can fail if the partials exist at a point but are not continuous nearby, so existence alone is not the hypothesis.

options: When the second partial derivatives are continuous, the Hessian is symmetric.
The second derivative of the slice \(t \mapsto f(x + t d)\) at 0 is \(d^{T} H d\), when \(H\) exists and is continuous.
The Hessian of a linear function is the identity.
Mixed partials are equal at a point whenever both of them exist there, with no extra hypothesis.

questions.prompt: For the Hessian \(\begin{bmatrix} 12 & 8 \\ 8 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\), what is the determinant?
questions.explanation: The determinant is \(12 \cdot 4 - 8 \cdot 8 = 48 - 64 = -16\). The product of the diagonal entries is 48, which forgets to subtract the off-diagonal product. The trace is 16. A negative determinant means the two eigenvalues have opposite signs, so the quadratic form is indefinite. The sign is part of the value.

questions.prompt: Along a segment, an increment of the gradient can be written with the Hessian because
questions.explanation: The fundamental theorem along a segment integrates a derivative. Applied to the gradient, that derivative is the Hessian times the direction of the segment. The gradient is constant only when the Hessian is zero. The Hessian need not be a multiple of the identity, and it is evaluated along the segment, so it can change with the point.
